style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare transliterations in amp with Strong's carried in notes; em-dashes used sparingly; transliterations ASCII-normalized relative to the lexicon's spellings. Ecclesiastes uses Elohim throughout — the divine name YHWH never appears in the book and is never inserted.
chapterNote: The book's second half opens by answering chapter 6's question -- who knows what is good for man? -- with a chain of 'better than' proverbs, and every one of them cuts against instinct: a good name over good oil, the day of death over the day of birth, the funeral over the feast, sorrow over laughter, the wise man's rebuke over the fool's song. The house of mourning teaches what the banquet hall hides. From verse 13 the counsel deepens: receive both the straight days and the crooked ones from the same hand, avoid the twin ditches of self-righteous perfectionism and defiant wickedness -- the man who fears God walks out past both -- and hold no illusions, for there is not one righteous man on earth who does good and never sins. The chapter closes with the Preacher's audit of his own search: wisdom's full depth stayed out of reach, the predatory woman proved more bitter than death, hardly one true man in a thousand turned up, and the root finding under it all is Eden's: God made mankind upright, and they have gone hunting for schemes.

1.text: A good name is better than the finest fragrant oil, and the day of death better than the day of one's birth.
1.amp: A good name [shem -- reputation, memorial] is better [tov] than precious ointment [shemen -- fragrant anointing oil]; and the day [yom] of death [mavet] than the day of one's birth [yalad].
1.notes: The Hebrew plays shem (H8034) against shemen (H8081), name against oil, one consonant apart: fragrance evaporates, reputation endures. Death's day outranks birth's because only at the end is the shem complete and safe from ruin.

2.text: Better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for death is the end of every man, and the living will lay it to heart.
2.amp: It is better [tov] to go to the house [bayith] of mourning [ebel], than to go to the house of feasting [mishteh -- the drinking-banquet]: for that is the end [soph] of all men [adam]; and the living [chay] will lay [natan] it to his heart [leb].
2.notes: ebel (H60) is the lamentation of a funeral, and mishteh (H4960) the drinking-feast: the funeral is the better classroom because it teaches the one syllabus no one escapes. 'Lay it to heart', natan (H5414) with leb (H3820): let the lesson actually land.

3.text: Sorrow is better than laughter, for by the sadness of the face the heart is made sound.
3.amp: Sorrow [kaas -- grief, vexation] is better [tov] than laughter [sechok]: for by the sadness of the countenance [panim -- the face] the heart [leb] is made better [yatab -- made good, made well].
3.notes: kaas (H3708), the grief-word of 1:18, here doing constructive work: yatab (H3190), to make good. A sober face can be the outward sign of a heart under repair; laughter can be the sign of one avoiding the shop.

4.text: The heart of the wise lives in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.
4.amp: The heart [leb] of the wise [chakam] is in the house [bayith] of mourning [ebel]; but the heart of fools [kesil] is in the house of mirth [simchah].
4.notes: Not where the body visits but where the leb (H3820) dwells: the chakam (H2450) keeps mortality in view even at the feast, while the kesil (H3684) keeps the party going even at the graveside.

5.text: Better to hear the rebuke of a wise man than to be a man listening to the song of fools.
5.amp: It is better [tov] to hear [shama] the rebuke [gearah] of the wise [chakam], than for a man [ish] to hear the song [shir] of fools [kesil].
5.notes: gearah (H1606) is a sharp rebuke, and shir (H7892) a song: the choice is between words that hurt and help or words that soothe and cost. shama (H8085), hearing with intent to obey, decides which voice profits.

6.text: For like the crackling of thorn-branches under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool. This also is vapor.
6.amp: For as the crackling [qol -- the sound, Heb.] of thorns [sirim] under a pot [sir], so is the laughter [sechok] of the fool [kesil]: this also is vapor [hebel].
6.notes: Another Hebrew pun: sirim, thorns, under a sir, a pot (both H5518 in the tagging) -- a fire of thorns flares loud, bright, and briefly, and the pot never boils. So the kesil's sechok (H7814): all noise, no heat, and gone.

7.text: Surely oppression can drive even a wise man mad, and a bribe rots the heart out of him.
7.amp: Surely oppression [osheq -- extortion] makes a wise man [chakam] mad [halal -- raving]; and a gift [mattanah -- a bribe] destroys [abad] the heart [leb].
7.notes: osheq (H6233), extortion suffered or practiced, can unhinge even the chakam, and the 'gift' (H4979) is the bribe that makes abad (H6), perish, happen to a leb (H3820) from the inside. Wisdom is real but corruptible; guard the guard.

8.text: Better the end of a matter than its beginning, and better a patient spirit than a proud one.
8.amp: Better [tov] is the end [acharit -- the final outcome] of a thing [dabar] than the beginning [reshith] thereof: and the patient [arek -- long, slow] in spirit [ruach] is better than the proud [gabah -- high, lofty] in spirit.
8.notes: acharit (H319) is the far end where outcomes live; reshith (H7225) the launch where speeches live. arek ruach, the long spirit, outlasts gabah ruach, the high one -- patience is built for the distance between the two.

9.text: Do not be hurried in your spirit into anger, for anger settles down and makes its home in the chest of fools.
9.amp: Be not hasty [bahal -- rushed, alarmed] in your spirit [ruach] to be angry [kaas]: for anger [kaas] rests [nuach -- settles, takes up residence] in the bosom [cheq -- the lap, the chest] of fools [kesil].
9.notes: bahal (H926), the same rushed-word as 5:2, now about temper. nuach (H5117) is to settle and remain: in the kesil, anger is not a visitor but a tenant, housed in the cheq (H2436), the innermost lap.

10.text: Do not say, 'Why is it that the former days were better than these?' For it is not out of wisdom that you ask it.
10.amp: Say [amar] not thou, 'What is the cause that the former [rishon] days [yom] were better [tov] than these?' for you do not enquire [shaal] out of wisdom [chokmah -- 'out of wisdom', the KJV margin] concerning this.
10.notes: Nostalgia poses as insight and is neither: the question flatters the past, indicts providence, and excuses the present. shaal (H7592), to inquire: the asking itself, not the answer, is what wisdom faults.

11.text: Wisdom is good like an inheritance, and better still: an advantage to all who see the sun.
11.amp: Wisdom [chokmah] is good [tov] with an inheritance [nachalah] -- 'as good as an inheritance, yea, better too', the KJV margin: and by it there is profit [yother -- advantage] to them that see [raah] the sun [shemesh].
11.notes: nachalah (H5159) is the estate passed down; chokmah (H2451) matches it and outperforms it, for the comparison continues in verse 12. yother (H3148), the advantage-word, finally lands on something that holds it.

12.text: For wisdom is a shelter as money is a shelter, but the advantage of knowledge is this: wisdom keeps alive the one who has it.
12.amp: For wisdom [chokmah] is a defence [tsel -- a shadow, a shade, Heb.], and money [keseph] is a defence: but the excellency [yithron] of knowledge [daat] is, that wisdom gives life [chayah -- preserves alive] to them that have [baal -- own] it.
12.notes: Both are a tsel (H6738), a shade against the heat of trouble, the desert traveler's word for shelter. But keseph (H3701) can only cushion a life; chokmah can chayah (H2421) it, keep it alive -- the yithron (H3504), the surplus, at last has a column that pays.

13.text: Consider the work of God: who can straighten what He has made crooked?
13.amp: Consider [raah] the work [maaseh] of God [Elohim]: for who can [yakol] make that straight [taqan], which He has made crooked [avat]?
13.notes: The riddle of 1:15 returns with its authorship revealed: the crooked thing was made so by God. taqan (H8626) and avat (H5791), the straightening and the bending: some bends in your road are His workmanship, and the wise response is raah (H7200), consider, not renovate.

14.text: In the day of good, be in the good of it; and in the day of adversity, look hard: God has made the one right alongside the other, so that man can discover nothing of what comes after him.
14.amp: In the day [yom] of prosperity [tov] be joyful [tov -- be in the good], but in the day of adversity [ra] consider [raah]: God [Elohim] also has set [asah -- made] the one over against the other, to the end that man [adam] should find [matsa] nothing after [achar] him.
14.notes: The Hebrew doubles tov (H2896): in the good day, be in good. Both kinds of day come off the same workbench, asah (H6213), made -- and their alternation keeps the future unguessable, so that man leans on the Maker rather than the forecast (cf. Job 2:10).

15.text: I have seen it all in my vapor of days: there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man whose evil life runs long.
15.amp: All things have I seen [raah] in the days [yom] of my vapor [hebel]: there is [yesh] a just [tsaddiq] man that perishes [abad] in his righteousness [tsedek], and there is a wicked [rasha] man that prolongs [arak] his life in his wickedness [ra].
15.notes: The observation that breaks every tidy theology of reward: the tsaddiq (H6662) dies early and the rasha (H7563) grows old. abad (H6) and arak (H748), perishing and prolonging, land on the wrong men -- under the sun, the ledger does not settle on schedule.

16.text: Do not be righteous to excess, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you be left desolate?
16.amp: Be not righteous [tsaddiq] over much [rabah]; neither make yourself over [yother] wise [chakam]: why should you destroy yourself [shamem -- be desolate, appalled]?
16.notes: Not a warning against real holiness but against its counterfeit: the self-manufactured righteousness that trusts its own audit (cf. Luke 18:11-12). shamem (H8074), to be left desolate: perfectionism promises safety and delivers ruin.

17.text: Do not be wicked to excess either, and do not play the fool. Why should you die before your time?
17.amp: Be not over much [rabah] wicked [rasha], neither be thou foolish [sakal]: why should you die [muth] before your time [et -- 'not in thy time', the KJV margin]?
17.notes: The other ditch: since no one is sinless (v. 20), some conclude sin freely -- and rasha (H7561) as a career shortens the road. The et (H6256), the appointed time, can be forfeited early by the fool determined to find out.

18.text: It is good to take hold of the one warning without letting go of the other, for the man who fears God comes out past them both.
18.amp: It is good [tov] that you should take hold [achaz -- grasp firmly] of this; yea, also from this withdraw [yanach] not your hand: for he that fears [yare] God [Elohim] shall come forth [yatsa] of them all.
18.notes: achaz (H270), the grasping-word: hold both rails, the warning against self-righteousness and the warning against license. The yare Elohim (H3373), the God-fearer, is the man who walks out, yatsa (H3318), past both ditches -- fear of God is the book's road between them.

19.text: Wisdom makes the wise man stronger than ten rulers who hold power in a city.
19.amp: Wisdom [chokmah] strengthens [azaz -- makes strong, prevails] the wise [chakam] more than ten [eser] mighty rulers which are in the city [ir].
19.notes: azaz (H5810), to be strong and prevail: one chakam with chokmah outweighs a full bench of shallitim, the empowered men of the ir (H5892). Compare the poor wise man of 9:14-15 who saves a city the mighty could not.

20.text: Indeed, there is not one righteous man on the earth who always does good and never sins.
20.amp: For there is not a just [tsaddiq] man [adam] upon earth [eretz], that does [asah] good [tov], and sins [chet] not.
20.notes: The verse Paul builds into his indictment of the whole race (cf. Romans 3:10): tsaddiq (H6662) without chet (H2398) does not exist on eretz (H776). This is the floor under verses 16-18 -- no one escapes by performance.

21.text: And do not give your heart to every word men speak, or you may hear your own servant calling a curse down on you;
21.amp: Also take no heed ['give not thine heart', leb, the KJV margin] unto all words [dabar] that are spoken [dabar]; lest you hear [shama] your servant [ebed] curse [qalal -- treat as light, revile] you:
21.notes: qalal (H7043) is to make light of, to revile: eavesdroppers hear their own weight measured. The counsel is a mercy -- do not natan the leb (H3820), hand your heart over, to every stray sentence about you.

22.text: for your own heart knows that many times you yourself have done the same, and cursed others.
22.amp: For oftentimes [many times, paam rav] also your own heart [leb] knows [yada] that you yourself likewise have cursed [qalal] others [acher].
22.notes: The mirror-clause: the leb (H3820) keeps receipts. yada (H3045), it knows -- the surest cure for resenting other men's tongues is an honest audit of one's own.

23.text: All this I put to the proof by wisdom. I said, 'I will be wise,' but it stayed far away from me.
23.amp: All this have I proved [nasah -- tested] by wisdom [chokmah]: I said [amar], 'I will be wise [chakam]'; but it was far [rachoq] from me.
23.notes: nasah (H5254), the testing-word of 2:1, now aimed at wisdom itself. The resolve 'I will be chakam' met a horizon: rachoq (H7350), far off -- the more wisdom he gained, the further its fullness receded.

24.text: Whatever is, lies far off and deep, deep down. Who can find it out?
24.amp: That which is far off [rachoq], and exceeding deep [amoq amoq -- deep, deep], who can find it out [matsa]?
24.notes: The Hebrew doubles the depth-word (H6013): deep, deep. Reality's full account is both rachoq (H7350), beyond reach outward, and amoq, beyond reach downward; matsa (H4672), the finding-verb, will toll through the rest of the chapter mostly in the negative.

25.text: I turned, and my heart with me, to know and to explore and to seek out wisdom and the reckoning of things, and to know the wickedness of folly, the foolishness that is madness.
25.amp: I applied ['I and mine heart compassed', savav, the KJV margin] my heart [leb] to know [yada], and to search [tur], and to seek out [baqash] wisdom [chokmah], and the reason [cheshbon -- the account, the reckoning] of things, and to know the wickedness [resha] of folly [kesel], even of foolishness [sikhluth] and madness [holelut]:
25.notes: cheshbon (H2808) is an accountant's word, the sum or scheme of things; tur (H8446) the scout's word again. The search now includes the dark wing of the library: resha (H7562), folly, sikhluth (H5531), and holelut (H1947) -- he studied evil to know it, not to join it.

26.text: And I found something more bitter than death: the woman whose heart is snares and nets, whose hands are shackles. The man who is good before God escapes her, but the sinner is caught by her.
26.amp: And I find [matsa] more bitter [mar] than death [mavet] the woman [ishshah] whose heart [leb] is snares and nets [cherem -- the hunting-net], and her hands as bands [esur -- fetters]: whoso pleases God ['he that is good before God', tov, panim, the KJV margin] shall escape [malat] from her; but the sinner [chet] shall be taken [lakad] by her.
26.notes: Not womankind but the predator-figure Proverbs calls the strange woman (cf. Proverbs 5:3-5; 7:22-27): leb as trap, hands as esur (H612), fetters. malat (H4422), to slip away, belongs to the man who is tov before God's face; the chet (H2398) walks into the cherem (H2764), the net, on his own feet.

27.text: 'Look, this I have found,' says the Preacher, 'adding one thing to another to reach the reckoning:
27.amp: Behold [raah], this have I found [matsa], says [amar] the preacher [Qoheleth], counting one [echad] by one, to find out the account [cheshbon -- 'weighing one thing after another, to find out the reason', the KJV margin]:
27.notes: The Convener shows his method: echad by echad (H259), item by item, toward the cheshbon (H2808), the audited total. The bookkeeping frame is honest -- and the next verse reports how short the count came up.

28.text: which my soul is seeking still, and I have not found. One man among a thousand I have found, but a woman among all those I have not found.
28.amp: Which yet my soul [nephesh] seeks [baqash], but I find [matsa] not: one [echad] man [adam] among a thousand [eleph] have I found; but a woman [ishshah] among all those have I not found.
28.notes: In the harem-court of chapter 2's king -- where women were collected as possessions -- the sample was poisoned by the collecting; the finding indicts his world and his own part in it as much as anyone in it. One true adam in an eleph (H505): the count of the upright approaches zero from both sides, setting up verse 29's universal verdict.

29.text: Look, this alone I have found: that God made mankind upright, but they have gone seeking out many schemes.'
29.amp: Lo [raah], this only [bad -- alone] have I found [matsa], that God [Elohim] has made [asah] man [adam] upright [yashar -- straight]; but they have sought out [baqash] many [rav] inventions [chishshebonot -- schemes, contrivances].
29.notes: The one solid finding, and it is Genesis: adam left the Maker's hand yashar (H3477), straight, and the crookedness of 7:13 entered by man's own baqash (H1245), his seeking. The 'inventions' (H2810) share a root with verse 27's cheshbon: made to calculate, man calculates his way from God.
